box-step-up-dbs.name: Box Step-Up (DBs)
box-step-up-dbs.execution: Hold DBs at the sides, standing facing a knee-height box. Place one whole foot on the box, drive through that heel to stand tall on top (bringing the trailing leg up or into a knee drive). Lower under control back to the floor with the same leg leading. Complete reps, then switch.
box-step-up-dbs.why: Trains concentric single-leg hip and knee extension against load through a functional step pattern, building unilateral pushing strength and the controlled eccentric needed to lower the body on one leg.
box-step-up-dbs.transfer: Builds the single-leg extension power used to drive each stride and accelerate, and the controlled single-leg lowering that mirrors absorbing load on one edge during turns and stops.
box-step-up-dbs.cues: "Whole foot on the box, drive the heel" · "stand tall, don’t push off the bottom foot" · "lower slow"
box-step-up-dbs.mistakes: Pushing off the trailing toe (cheating); knee caving; box too high (hips rise above knee, leaning)
box-step-up-dbs.progression: Progress: heavier DBs or add a knee drive/jump | Regress: lower box or bodyweight

sl-box-step-down.name: SL Box Step-Down
sl-box-step-down.execution: Stand on top of a low box on one leg, the other leg hanging off the edge. Slowly bend the standing leg to lower the free heel toward the floor under control, keeping the standing knee tracking over the foot and the hips level. Lightly tap the floor (or hover), then drive back up to standing. Reps, then switch.
sl-box-step-down.why: Emphasizes the eccentric (lowering) phase of single-leg knee/hip control, building strength in the lengthening muscles and training the knee to resist valgus collapse under deceleration loads.
sl-box-step-down.transfer: Trains the controlled single-leg deceleration used when stopping, slowing into turns, and landing; building eccentric knee control improves edge stability and protects the knee on hard direction changes.
sl-box-step-down.cues: "Lower slow, knee over the toes" · "hips stay level" · "tap, don’t crash"
sl-box-step-down.mistakes: Dropping too fast (no control); knee caving in; hips hiking or dropping to the free side
sl-box-step-down.progression: Progress: higher box or hold a DB | Regress: lower box or reduce range
sl-box-step-down.muscles: Quads, glutes, gluteus medius, hip stabilizers
sl-box-step-down.nameHint: Сход с тумбы на одной ноге

sl-balance-eyes-open.name: SL Balance — Eyes Open
sl-balance-eyes-open.execution: Stand on one leg, the other knee lifted to around hip height or the foot held just off the floor. Find a focal point, stack the hips level, and hold a tall, quiet posture. Keep a soft standing knee and let the foot and ankle make small corrections. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch.
sl-balance-eyes-open.why: Challenges the ankle, knee, and hip proprioceptive and stabilizing systems to maintain single-leg balance, training the small postural muscles and neuromuscular control that underpin all single-leg actions.
sl-balance-eyes-open.transfer: Builds the single-leg balance and ankle/hip stability required to glide and push on one edge; better proprioception improves stride stability and the ability to recover balance after contact.
sl-balance-eyes-open.cues: "Tall and quiet" · "hips level" · "let the foot make small fixes"
sl-balance-eyes-open.mistakes: Hips dropping to the free side; gripping/clawing excessively; locking the standing knee
sl-balance-eyes-open.progression: Progress: eyes closed or unstable surface | Regress: hold a light support or shorten the time

banded-standing-adduction.name: Banded Standing Adduction
banded-standing-adduction.execution: Anchor a band at ankle height to a post and loop it around the inside ankle of the working leg; stand side-on so the band pulls the leg outward. Stabilize on the outside leg, then pull the banded leg across the midline (adduction) against the band, and control it back out. Keep the torso tall and pelvis stable. Reps, then switch.
banded-standing-adduction.why: Directly strengthens the adductors through their primary action — pulling the leg toward and across the midline — against resistance, building inner-thigh strength that is frequently underdeveloped and injury-prone.
banded-standing-adduction.transfer: Strengthens the adductors that decelerate and contribute to the skating stride and stabilize the hips on edges; targeted adductor strength is a key strategy to prevent the common groin strains in hockey.
banded-standing-adduction.cues: "Pull from the inner thigh" · "tall posture, still pelvis" · "control it back out"
banded-standing-adduction.mistakes: Twisting the torso/pelvis to cheat; swinging with momentum; band too heavy to control
banded-standing-adduction.progression: Progress: heavier band or slower tempo | Regress: lighter band or reduce range

split-squat.name: Split Squat
split-squat.execution: Set up in a split stance, front foot flat, rear foot back on the ball of the foot. Brace and lower straight down by bending both knees until the back knee nears the floor and the front thigh is near parallel, front shin vertical. Drive through the front foot to stand. Complete reps, then switch.
split-squat.why: A stationary single-leg pattern that loads the front leg’s quad and glute through a controlled range with a stable base, building unilateral strength and balance with less coordination demand than walking variations.
split-squat.transfer: Builds the single-leg quad/glute strength behind stride push-off and the split-stance stability used in low, staggered athletic positions; a foundational unilateral strength builder for skating power.
split-squat.cues: "Drop straight down" · "front shin vertical, weight in the heel" · "tall torso"
split-squat.mistakes: Front knee caving or jutting forward; torso leaning forward; pushing off the back foot
split-squat.progression: Progress: hold DBs or elevate the rear foot (Bulgarian) | Regress: shorten range or hold a support

banded-lateral-lunge.name: Banded Lateral Lunge
banded-lateral-lunge.execution: Loop a band for resistance (around the working leg or held) and stand tall. Step wide to one side, bending that knee and pushing the hips back while the trailing leg stays straight, feet flat. Descend to a comfortable depth against band tension, then drive back to center against the band. Reps, then switch.
banded-lateral-lunge.why: Adds accommodating resistance to the lateral lunge, loading the frontal-plane hip and adductors through the push back to center, building lateral push strength and hip/adductor control with a joint-friendly stimulus.
banded-lateral-lunge.transfer: Trains the lateral push-off and return of the crossover and stride directly in the frontal plane; resisted adductor/glute loading improves side-to-side push power and protects against groin/hip strain.
banded-lateral-lunge.cues: "Sit back into the hip" · "heel down, toes forward" · "drive back against the band"
banded-lateral-lunge.mistakes: Heel lifting; chest collapsing; knee caving; losing band tension
banded-lateral-lunge.progression: Progress: heavier band or add a DB | Regress: lighter band or bodyweight lateral lunge

db-bulgarian-split-squat.name: DB Bulgarian Split Squat
db-bulgarian-split-squat.execution: Hold DBs at the sides with the top of the rear foot on a bench a stride behind. Brace and lower the back knee toward the floor by bending the front leg, front shin near vertical, torso slightly forward. Descend until the front thigh nears parallel, then drive through the front foot to stand. Reps, then switch.
db-bulgarian-split-squat.why: Loading the rear-foot-elevated split squat with DBs heavily overloads single-leg quad and glute strength through a long range, with a high balance and stability demand — one of the most effective unilateral strength builders.
db-bulgarian-split-squat.transfer: Builds maximal single-leg push-off strength specific to the stride and the unilateral stability that supports edges and turns; deep loaded range develops stride power and knee/hip resilience.
db-bulgarian-split-squat.cues: "Down toward the floor" · "weight in the front heel" · "control down, drive up"
db-bulgarian-split-squat.mistakes: Front knee caving; standing too close; rushing the eccentric; torso collapsing
db-bulgarian-split-squat.progression: Progress: heavier DBs or tempo/pause | Regress: lighter DBs, lower elevation, or bodyweight

sl-balance-eyes-closed.name: SL Balance — Eyes Closed
sl-balance-eyes-closed.execution: Stand on one leg with the other foot lifted, find a tall posture, then close the eyes. Maintain a level pelvis and tall spine, letting the foot and ankle make constant small corrections without vision. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch sides. Stand near a wall for safety.
sl-balance-eyes-closed.why: Removing visual input forces reliance on the vestibular and proprioceptive systems, sharply increasing the demand on ankle, knee, and hip stabilizers and training balance control where vision can’t compensate.
sl-balance-eyes-closed.transfer: Builds the deep proprioceptive single-leg control needed to stay balanced on an edge and recover from off-balance contact; training without vision improves stability when the eyes are tracking the puck or play.
sl-balance-eyes-closed.cues: "Tall and quiet, breathe" · "hips level" · "trust the foot to correct"
sl-balance-eyes-closed.mistakes: Hopping or putting the foot down quickly; hips dropping; tensing the whole body rigidly
sl-balance-eyes-closed.progression: Progress: unstable surface or add a head turn | Regress: open eyes or lightly touch a support
sl-balance-eyes-closed.nameHint: Баланс на одной ноге — глаза закрыты

push-up.name: Push-Up
push-up.execution: Set hands slightly wider than the shoulders, body in a straight line from head to heels, core and glutes braced. Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows at ~45° to the torso until the chest nearly touches, then press back up to full extension. Keep the hips level and neck neutral throughout.
push-up.why: A closed-chain horizontal press that builds chest, shoulder, and triceps strength while demanding full-body tension and scapular control — training pressing strength and a rigid, braced trunk simultaneously.
push-up.transfer: Builds the upper-body pushing strength and trunk stiffness used to fend off opponents, win body position, and absorb contact; scapular control supports shoulder durability in checks and falls.
push-up.cues: "Straight line, squeeze glutes" · "elbows ~45°, not flared" · "full lockout at the top"
push-up.mistakes: Hips sagging or piking; elbows flaring to 90°; partial range (chest not lowering enough)
push-up.progression: Progress: deficit, feet elevated, or weighted | Regress: hands elevated or from the knees

db-floor-press.name: DB Floor Press
db-floor-press.execution: Lie on the floor, knees bent, a DB in each hand pressed up over the chest. Lower the DBs until the upper arms (triceps) rest lightly on the floor, elbows at ~45°, then press back up to lockout, keeping the wrists stacked over the elbows. Control each rep; the floor limits the range.
db-floor-press.why: The floor caps the range at the elbows, reducing shoulder strain while emphasizing the triceps-lockout portion and chest contraction; builds horizontal pressing strength safely with a built-in pause at the bottom.
db-floor-press.transfer: Develops upper-body pressing strength for puck battles, shoving for position, and stick-on-puck strength, while the limited range is shoulder-friendly for players managing shoulder load.
db-floor-press.cues: "Stack wrists over elbows" · "light touch, then press" · "drive the DBs together at the top"
db-floor-press.mistakes: Elbows flaring wide; bouncing the arms off the floor; uneven press (one side leading)
db-floor-press.progression: Progress: heavier DBs or single-arm (anti-rotation) | Regress: lighter DBs or one arm at a time slowly

half-kneeling-db-press.name: Half-Kneeling DB Press
half-kneeling-db-press.execution: Half-kneeling (one knee down, opposite foot forward), DB racked at the shoulder on the down-knee side. Brace the core and glutes, ribs down, and press the DB straight overhead to lockout without leaning back. Lower under control to the shoulder. Complete reps, then switch sides/knees.
half-kneeling-db-press.why: The half-kneeling base removes leg drive and challenges the core to resist arching and leaning, building honest vertical pressing strength and shoulder stability while training anti-extension trunk control.
half-kneeling-db-press.transfer: Builds overhead and shoulder pressing strength with trunk stability transferable to absorbing contact and protecting the puck with extended arms; the anti-lean demand reinforces core stiffness in battles.
half-kneeling-db-press.cues: "Ribs down, glute tight" · "press straight up, not back" · "stack the wrist over the elbow"
half-kneeling-db-press.mistakes: Arching the low back to press; leaning the torso back; pressing the DB forward of the head
half-kneeling-db-press.progression: Progress: heavier DB or tall-kneeling/standing | Regress: lighter DB or seated for stability
half-kneeling-db-press.nameHint: Жим гантели стоя на одном колене

db-push-up-to-row.name: DB Push-Up to Row
db-push-up-to-row.execution: In a push-up position gripping two DBs, feet wide for stability and body in a straight line. Perform a push-up, then at the top row one DB to the ribs while bracing hard against rotation, lower it, and row the other side. Keep the hips square and level throughout. Alternate rows.
db-push-up-to-row.why: Pairs a horizontal press with a single-arm row under a heavy anti-rotation demand — the body must resist twisting as one hand lifts, building pressing and pulling strength plus rotary core stiffness simultaneously.
db-push-up-to-row.transfer: Builds balanced push/pull upper-body strength and the anti-rotation core stiffness used to stay square in board battles and resist being turned; trains trunk control while one arm is occupied on the puck.
db-push-up-to-row.cues: "Hips square, don’t twist" · "feet wide for a stable base" · "row to the ribs, control down"
db-push-up-to-row.mistakes: Hips rocking/rotating with each row; flaring the press; feet too narrow (unstable)
db-push-up-to-row.progression: Progress: heavier DBs or feet closer | Regress: row only (no push-up) or from the knees
db-push-up-to-row.muscles: Pectorals, lats, triceps, biceps, anti-rotation core

plyo-push-up-knees.name: Plyo Push-Up (Knees)
plyo-push-up-knees.execution: From a knee push-up position, body straight from knees to head, lower the chest with control, then press explosively enough for the hands to leave the floor. Land softly with bent elbows and immediately absorb into the next rep. Keep the core braced and avoid hip sag.
plyo-push-up-knees.why: Introduces the stretch-shortening cycle to upper-body pressing at a manageable load (knees), training rate of force development and explosive concentric power in the pressing muscles with soft, controlled landings.
plyo-push-up-knees.transfer: Develops explosive upper-body push power for the first forceful shove in a battle and quick hand recovery; the reactive press trains fast force production used in contact and pushing off the boards.
plyo-push-up-knees.cues: "Explode off the floor" · "soft, bent-elbow landing" · "stay tight, no hip sag"
plyo-push-up-knees.mistakes: Hips sagging; stiff/locked-elbow landings; pressing slowly (no real push-off)
plyo-push-up-knees.progression: Progress: full plyo push-up (feet down) or clap | Regress: fast concentric without leaving the floor

clap-push-up-or-hard-plyo.name: Clap Push-Up (or Hard Plyo)
clap-push-up-or-hard-plyo.execution: From a full push-up position, body straight and braced, lower the chest with control, then press explosively so the hands leave the floor enough to clap (or just leave the floor for a hard plyo). Land softly on bent elbows and absorb directly into the next rep. Keep the hips level throughout.
clap-push-up-or-hard-plyo.why: A high-output plyometric press demanding maximal rate of force development to project the body off the floor; trains explosive concentric pressing power and reactive landing absorption through a full stretch-shortening cycle.
clap-push-up-or-hard-plyo.transfer: Builds maximal explosive upper-body push power for the forceful first shove in contact and board battles, and the reactive strength to absorb and redirect force quickly through the arms and trunk.
clap-push-up-or-hard-plyo.cues: "Push the floor away violently" · "catch soft, elbows bend" · "reset tight each rep"
clap-push-up-or-hard-plyo.mistakes: Hips sagging; landing stiff (jarring the wrists/elbows); insufficient push-off to leave the floor
clap-push-up-or-hard-plyo.progression: Progress: multiple claps or a weighted vest | Regress: plyo push-up from the knees

plank-to-push-up.name: Plank to Push-Up
plank-to-push-up.execution: Start in a forearm plank, body straight and braced. Press up onto one hand, then the other, into a full push-up position, then lower back down to the forearms one arm at a time. Keep the hips as square and still as possible — minimize side-to-side rocking. Alternate the leading arm each rep.
plank-to-push-up.why: Combines a press-up transition with a strong anti-rotation demand; resisting the hips’ tendency to rock as each arm moves builds shoulder stability, triceps strength, and rotary core control under a moving base.
plank-to-push-up.transfer: Trains the anti-rotation trunk stiffness used to stay square and resist being turned in battles, plus shoulder stability while transferring weight between arms — relevant to balance during contact.
plank-to-push-up.cues: "Hips quiet, don’t rock" · "press through the whole hand" · "brace before each transition"
plank-to-push-up.mistakes: Hips rocking side to side; sagging or piking; rushing and losing the brace
plank-to-push-up.progression: Progress: feet closer or add a tempo | Regress: from the knees or slow the transitions

deficit-push-up.name: Deficit Push-Up
deficit-push-up.execution: Place each hand on a low surface (low blocks, books, or plates) a bit wider than the shoulders, body in a straight line and braced. Lower the chest between the hands below hand level for an extended range, then press back to full lockout. Keep the elbows at ~45°, hips level, neck neutral. Control the deeper descent.
deficit-push-up.why: Increasing the range below the hands lengthens the pecs and front delts under load (greater eccentric stretch), raising time under tension and building pressing strength through a fuller range than a floor push-up.
deficit-push-up.transfer: Builds pressing strength through a deep range for fending off and shoving in battles; the added stretch under load develops chest/shoulder strength useful in extended-arm puck protection and contact.
deficit-push-up.cues: "Chest sinks below the hands" · "elbows ~45°, stay tight" · "full press to lockout"
deficit-push-up.mistakes: Hips sagging into the deeper range; elbows flaring; bouncing out of the bottom
deficit-push-up.progression: Progress: greater deficit or add load | Regress: standard floor push-up or hands elevated

archer-push-up.name: Archer Push-Up
archer-push-up.execution: Set the hands wide, body straight and braced. Lower toward one hand by bending that elbow while the opposite arm stays nearly straight, sliding the weight onto the working side. Press back to center, then alternate. Keep the hips square and level; control the shift to each side.
archer-push-up.why: Shifts most of the load onto one arm, approaching a one-arm press stimulus; builds unilateral pressing strength and the trunk control to resist sagging and rotation as load moves side to side.
archer-push-up.transfer: Develops near single-arm pushing strength and anti-rotation trunk stiffness used to shove one-handed in battles and stay square; bridges toward stronger one-arm pressing for contact.
archer-push-up.cues: "Sink to one hand, other arm long" · "hips square, don’t twist" · "control the shift"
archer-push-up.mistakes: Hips rotating or sagging; the straight arm bending to cheat; rushing the side shift
archer-push-up.progression: Progress: more weight on the working arm toward a one-arm push-up | Regress: from the knees or reduce the shift
archer-push-up.muscles: Pectorals, triceps, anterior deltoids, anti-rotation core

banded-chest-press.name: Banded Chest Press
banded-chest-press.execution: Anchor a band behind you at chest height (or loop it across the upper back), a handle in each hand at the chest, in a staggered stance for balance. Press the hands forward to full extension against the band, squeezing the chest, then return under control to the chest. Keep the torso upright and braced.
banded-chest-press.why: Provides accommodating horizontal pressing resistance that peaks at lockout, training the chest, front delts, and triceps where tension matches the strengthening leverage; joint-friendly and standing, so the trunk stabilizes the press.
banded-chest-press.transfer: Builds the horizontal push strength used to shove opponents and create space in battles, trained standing so the core stabilizes the press the way it must on the ice during contact.
banded-chest-press.cues: "Press through the chest" · "stay tall, brace the core" · "control it back in"
banded-chest-press.mistakes: Leaning the whole body into the press; shrugging the shoulders; letting the band snap back
banded-chest-press.progression: Progress: heavier band or single-arm (anti-rotation) | Regress: lighter band or shorter range

push-up-to-reach.name: Push-Up to Reach
push-up-to-reach.execution: Perform a push-up; at the top, lift one hand and reach it forward (or out in front) while bracing hard to keep the hips square, then return the hand and repeat on the other side. Keep the body in a straight line, hips level — no rocking. Alternate the reaching arm each rep.
push-up-to-reach.why: Adds an anti-rotation and single-arm support demand at the top of each rep; reaching one arm forward loads the supporting shoulder’s serratus and stabilizers while the core resists rotation, building shoulder stability and trunk stiffness.
push-up-to-reach.transfer: Trains shoulder stability and anti-rotation control while one arm is extended — mirroring reaching with the stick or a one-arm position during puck protection while staying square against pressure.
push-up-to-reach.cues: "Hips square through the reach" · "reach long, stay tight" · "control back to the hand"
push-up-to-reach.mistakes: Hips rocking or rotating during the reach; sagging; rushing the reach
push-up-to-reach.progression: Progress: longer reach or hold at the top | Regress: shorter reach or from the knees
push-up-to-reach.muscles: Pectorals, triceps, serratus anterior, anti-rotation core

explosive-push-up.name: Explosive Push-Up
explosive-push-up.execution: From a full push-up position, body braced, lower with control, then press up as fast and forcefully as possible — driving the hands hard into the floor so the press is explosive (the hands may leave the floor slightly). Reset and repeat with intent on every concentric. Keep the hips level and core tight.
explosive-push-up.why: Maximizing concentric velocity recruits high-threshold motor units and trains rate of force development in the pressing muscles; emphasizing intent-to-move-fast builds explosive pushing power even without a full plyometric catch.
explosive-push-up.transfer: Develops the fast, forceful upper-body push used to shove off opponents and the boards and to win the first contact in a battle; trains the nervous system to express strength quickly.
explosive-push-up.cues: "Drive the floor away fast" · "every press explosive" · "stay tight, hips level"
explosive-push-up.mistakes: Pressing slowly (no intent); hips sagging; sacrificing range to go faster
explosive-push-up.progression: Progress: hands leave the floor / plyo or clap push-up | Regress: standard push-up with fast intent or from the knees

band-chest-pass.name: Band Chest Pass
band-chest-pass.execution: Anchor a band behind you, handles at the chest, in a staggered athletic stance. Explosively press both hands forward to full extension as fast as possible (like a two-hand chest pass), then control the return. Reset posture each rep and press with maximal intent. Brace the trunk against the band’s pull.
band-chest-pass.why: A ballistic horizontal press against accommodating resistance, training maximal concentric velocity and rate of force development in the pressing chain; the explosive intent develops upper-body power specific to pushing actions.
band-chest-pass.transfer: Mirrors the explosive two-arm push used to shove opponents off the puck and create space along the boards; builds the fast horizontal force production used in contact.
band-chest-pass.cues: "Punch the hands out fast" · "athletic base, brace" · "control the return"
band-chest-pass.mistakes: Pressing slowly; lunging the body forward instead of the arms; losing posture
band-chest-pass.progression: Progress: heavier band or single-arm | Regress: lighter band or non-ballistic press

db-push-press.name: DB Push Press
db-push-press.execution: Stand with DBs racked at the shoulders, feet hip-width. Brace, perform a quick shallow dip at the knees and hips, then explosively extend the legs to drive the DBs overhead, finishing with the arms locked out and ribs down. Lower under control to the shoulders. Keep the torso upright through the dip-drive.
db-push-press.why: Uses leg drive (triple extension of the ankles, knees, hips) to launch the load overhead, training full-body power transfer from the ground through the trunk to the arms and allowing heavier loading than a strict press.
db-push-press.transfer: Trains explosive lower-to-upper power transfer and triple extension that underpin a powerful stride push-off and the ability to generate force from the legs through a braced trunk in contact and battles.
db-push-press.cues: "Quick dip, big drive" · "ribs down, finish tall" · "punch through the legs"
db-push-press.mistakes: Dipping too deep or slow (squatting); pressing before the legs drive; arching the low back at lockout
db-push-press.progression: Progress: heavier DBs or single-arm | Regress: lighter DBs or strict overhead press

band-pull-apart.name: Band Pull-Apart
band-pull-apart.execution: Hold a band with both hands in front at shoulder height, arms straight. Pull the band apart by driving the hands out to the sides, squeezing the shoulder blades together, until the band touches or nears the chest. Pause, then return under control. Keep the ribs down and shoulders away from the ears.
band-pull-apart.why: Strengthens the scapular retractors (mid-traps, rhomboids) and rear delts through horizontal abduction, improving posture and the front-to-back shoulder balance that pressing-heavy athletes often lack.
band-pull-apart.transfer: Builds rear-shoulder and upper-back strength that stabilizes the shoulder for shooting, passing, and absorbing checks; improved scapular control supports shoulder durability and strong posture in skating.
band-pull-apart.cues: "Squeeze the shoulder blades" · "ribs down, shoulders down" · "control it back in"
band-pull-apart.mistakes: Shrugging the shoulders up; bending the elbows; using momentum or jerking
band-pull-apart.progression: Progress: heavier band or pause at end range | Regress: lighter band or narrower grip

band-pull-apart-speed.name: Band Pull-Apart Speed
band-pull-apart-speed.execution: Hold the band in front at shoulder height, arms straight. Pull apart and return in a fast, rhythmic cadence, squeezing the shoulder blades on each rep while keeping the ribs down. Maintain crisp form at speed for the prescribed reps or time; don’t let the shoulders shrug up.
band-pull-apart-speed.why: Trains the scapular retractors and rear delts at higher velocity and rep volume, building rate of activation and muscular endurance in the postural muscles that hold the shoulders back under fatigue.
band-pull-apart-speed.transfer: Builds fast and endurance qualities in the rear shoulder and upper back that stabilize the shoulder during repeated shots, passes, and contacts across a shift, supporting durable posture.
band-pull-apart-speed.cues: "Fast but full squeeze" · "shoulders down, ribs down" · "crisp rhythm"
band-pull-apart-speed.mistakes: Shrugging at speed; shortening the range; losing the shoulder-blade squeeze
band-pull-apart-speed.progression: Progress: heavier band or longer sets | Regress: lighter band or slow-tempo pull-aparts

band-row.name: Band Row
band-row.execution: Anchor a band in front at chest or waist height, a handle in each hand, arms extended, in an athletic staggered or hip-width stance. Row the handles toward the ribs by driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades, then extend the arms under control. Keep the torso upright and braced; don’t lean back.
band-row.why: Strengthens the lats, rhomboids, mid-traps, and biceps through horizontal pulling, building the back strength and scapular control that balance pressing work and stabilize the shoulder girdle.
band-row.transfer: Builds the pulling and back strength used to control opponents’ sticks, tie up bodies, and win battles, plus the scapular stability that protects the shoulder during contact and supports strong shooting posture.
band-row.cues: "Elbows back, squeeze the blades" · "tall chest, don’t lean back" · "control the stretch"
band-row.mistakes: Leaning back to pull (using the torso); shrugging; not retracting the shoulder blades
band-row.progression: Progress: heavier band or single-arm (anti-rotation) | Regress: lighter band or shorter range
band-row.muscles: Lats, rhomboids, mid-traps, biceps, rear delts

hanging-bar-hold.name: Hanging / Bar Hold
hanging-bar-hold.execution: Grip a pull-up bar with hands shoulder-width, palms forward, and hang with the arms straight. Keep the shoulders lightly “packed” (not fully shrugged to the ears) and the core gently braced. Hold for the prescribed time, breathing steadily, then lower under control. Build the time gradually.
hanging-bar-hold.why: Builds grip strength-endurance and forearm/finger-flexor endurance under bodyweight load, while lightly decompressing the spine and training shoulder and scapular stability in a hanging position.
hanging-bar-hold.transfer: Develops the grip and forearm endurance used to control the stick through battles and a full game, and the strong hands that resist losing the stick when checked or tied up.
hanging-bar-hold.cues: "Pack the shoulders lightly" · "relax the breathing" · "build the time slowly"
hanging-bar-hold.mistakes: Fully dead-hanging the shoulders to the ears; swinging; a death grip while holding the breath
hanging-bar-hold.progression: Progress: longer hold, single-arm, or add load | Regress: feet lightly supported or shorter holds

band-face-pull.name: Band Face Pull
band-face-pull.execution: Anchor a band at upper-chest or face height. Hold it with both hands, arms extended, and pull the band toward the face by driving the elbows high and out to the sides, externally rotating so the hands finish beside the ears. Squeeze the upper back, then return under control. Keep the ribs down.
band-face-pull.why: Trains the rear delts, external rotators, and scapular upward rotators together, strengthening the often-weak posterior shoulder and improving the rotator-cuff balance and posture that protect the shoulder joint.
band-face-pull.transfer: Builds rear-shoulder and rotator-cuff strength that stabilizes the shoulder for shooting and checking and reduces shoulder injury risk; supports a strong, square upper-body posture on the ice.
band-face-pull.cues: "Elbows high and wide" · "hands to the ears, rotate" · "ribs down, squeeze the back"
band-face-pull.mistakes: Pulling low to the chest (losing the high-elbow path); shrugging; using momentum
band-face-pull.progression: Progress: heavier band or pause/external-rotation hold | Regress: lighter band or reduce range
band-face-pull.muscles: Rear deltoids, external rotators, mid/lower traps

banded-y-t-w.name: Banded Y-T-W
banded-y-t-w.execution: Hold a band with light tension, arms in front. Raise the arms overhead into a “Y” (thumbs up), return; pull out to a “T” (arms straight to the sides, squeezing the blades), return; then a “W” (elbows bent, driven down and back). Move slowly with the ribs down, leading with the shoulder blades through each shape.
banded-y-t-w.why: Targets the lower and mid traps, rear delts, and rotator cuff through three complementary angles, building scapular control and posterior-shoulder endurance — addressing common weaknesses that affect shoulder posture and health.
banded-y-t-w.transfer: Strengthens the small scapular and cuff muscles that stabilize the shoulder for shooting, passing, and contact; better scapular control improves shoulder durability and posture during skating.
banded-y-t-w.cues: "Lead with the shoulder blades" · "ribs down, slow control" · "light tension, clean shapes"
banded-y-t-w.mistakes: Shrugging the upper traps; arching the low back on the Y; rushing the shapes
banded-y-t-w.progression: Progress: heavier band or pause each position | Regress: lighter/no band, fewer reps
banded-y-t-w.muscles: Lower/mid traps, rear delts, rotator cuff

banded-wrist-work.name: Banded Wrist Work
banded-wrist-work.execution: Anchor a light band and loop it around the hand. Work the wrist through its actions against tension — flexion (curling the palm toward the forearm), extension (lifting the back of the hand), and radial/ulnar deviation or rotation — moving slowly through a full range. Keep the forearm supported and still; only the wrist moves. Switch hands.
banded-wrist-work.why: Strengthens the wrist flexors, extensors, and deviators through their direct actions, building forearm and wrist strength and resilience in the small muscles that control fine hand and wrist positions.
banded-wrist-work.transfer: Directly strengthens the wrists and forearms that drive and control the stick — supporting wrist-shot snap, puck handling, and stick strength in battles — and builds resilience against wrist/forearm overuse.
banded-wrist-work.cues: "Only the wrist moves" · "slow through full range" · "forearm stays still"
banded-wrist-work.mistakes: Moving the whole forearm; rushing; band too heavy to control through the range
banded-wrist-work.progression: Progress: heavier band or add holds | Regress: lighter band or reduce range
banded-wrist-work.muscles: Wrist flexors, wrist extensors, forearm muscles

banded-shoulder-cuff-rotation.name: Banded Shoulder Cuff Rotation
banded-shoulder-cuff-rotation.execution: Anchor a band at elbow height. With the working elbow tucked to the side and bent 90°, rotate the forearm outward against the band (external rotation), keeping the elbow pinned to the ribs, then control back in. For internal rotation, face the other way and rotate the forearm across the body. Keep the wrist neutral. Reps each direction and side.
banded-shoulder-cuff-rotation.why: Isolates the rotator-cuff muscles (especially the external rotators) through their primary action, building the cuff strength and balance that stabilize the humeral head in the socket and protect the shoulder.
banded-shoulder-cuff-rotation.transfer: Strengthens the rotator cuff that stabilizes the shoulder during shooting, passing, and the forces of body checking and falls — a key element of shoulder durability and injury resilience for hockey.
banded-shoulder-cuff-rotation.cues: "Elbow pinned to the ribs" · "rotate from the shoulder, wrist neutral" · "slow and controlled"
banded-shoulder-cuff-rotation.mistakes: Elbow drifting away from the body; using the wrist or torso to cheat; band too heavy
banded-shoulder-cuff-rotation.progression: Progress: heavier band or pause at end range | Regress: lighter band or smaller range

renegade-row.name: Renegade Row
renegade-row.execution: Start in a high plank gripping two DBs, feet wide for stability, body in a straight line and braced. Row one DB to the ribs by driving the elbow back while resisting any hip rotation, lower it under control, then row the other side. Keep the hips square and level throughout. Alternate rows.
renegade-row.why: Pairs a single-arm row with a strong anti-rotation plank demand; lifting one hand forces the core to resist twisting and the standing arm to stabilize, building pulling strength and rotary trunk stiffness simultaneously.
renegade-row.transfer: Builds the back and pulling strength used to control sticks and bodies plus the anti-rotation core stiffness to stay square in board battles while one hand is occupied on the puck or an opponent.
renegade-row.cues: "Hips square, don’t twist" · "feet wide, stable base" · "row to the ribs, control down"
renegade-row.mistakes: Hips rotating with each row; sagging or piking; feet too narrow (unstable)
renegade-row.progression: Progress: heavier DBs or feet closer | Regress: wider feet, lighter DBs, or from the knees
renegade-row.muscles: Lats, rhomboids, biceps, anti-rotation core, shoulders

dead-bug.name: Dead Bug
dead-bug.execution: Lie on your back, arms reaching toward the ceiling and knees bent 90° over the hips. Press the low back into the floor. Slowly lower the opposite arm and leg toward the floor, extending them while keeping the back flat, then return and switch sides. Move slowly, exhaling as the limbs lower. Keep the ribs down.
dead-bug.why: Trains anti-extension core control — the deep abdominals must keep the spine neutral and ribs down while the limbs create a lengthening, destabilizing load — building the trunk stiffness that transfers force without the low back compensating.
dead-bug.transfer: Builds the core stiffness that lets the legs and arms generate force (stride push, shot) without energy leaking through a soft trunk; protects the low back during skating and contact.
dead-bug.cues: "Low back glued to the floor" · "ribs down, exhale as you reach" · "slow, controlled limbs"
dead-bug.mistakes: Low back arching off the floor; rushing; holding the breath
dead-bug.progression: Progress: add a DB / longer levers or slow tempo | Regress: move one limb at a time or reduce range
dead-bug.muscles: Rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, hip flexors

dead-bug-with-db.name: Dead Bug with DB
dead-bug-with-db.execution: Lie on your back, knees bent 90° over the hips, holding a DB (or DBs) pressed toward the ceiling. Press the low back into the floor, then lower the opposite arm (with the DB) and leg toward the floor, keeping the back flat, and return. Switch sides. Move slowly and keep the ribs down throughout.
dead-bug-with-db.why: Adds external load to the lengthening levers, increasing the anti-extension demand on the deep core to keep the spine neutral; builds greater trunk stiffness and the strength to resist extension under load.
dead-bug-with-db.transfer: Builds a stiffer, stronger trunk that transfers leg and arm force efficiently during powerful skating and shooting and resists the low-back extension forces of contact, supporting force transfer and injury resilience.
dead-bug-with-db.cues: "Back flat, ribs down" · "control the load down slow" · "exhale as you reach"
dead-bug-with-db.mistakes: Low back arching as the load lowers; rushing; letting the DB pull the rib cage up
dead-bug-with-db.progression: Progress: heavier DB or both limbs simultaneously | Regress: lighter/no weight (bodyweight dead bug)
dead-bug-with-db.muscles: Rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, hip flexors, shoulders

side-plank.name: Side Plank
side-plank.execution: Lie on your side, forearm under the shoulder, legs stacked. Brace and lift the hips so the body forms a straight line from head to feet, supported on the forearm and the side of the lower foot. Keep the hips high and the top shoulder stacked over the bottom. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch sides.
side-plank.why: Trains anti-lateral-flexion — the lateral core (obliques, quadratus lumborum) and lateral hip stabilizers must resist the hips collapsing toward the floor, building frontal-plane trunk and hip stability.
side-plank.transfer: Builds the lateral core and hip stability that keep the torso stacked over a single skating edge and resist being knocked sideways in contact; supports balance during one-leg loading and turns.
side-plank.cues: "Hips high, body in a line" · "stack the shoulders and hips" · "brace, don’t sag"
side-plank.mistakes: Hips sagging toward the floor; rotating the torso; shoulder not stacked over the elbow
side-plank.progression: Progress: top leg raised, reach-through, or add a hold/load | Regress: from the knees or shorten the hold
side-plank.muscles: Obliques, quadratus lumborum, gluteus medius, shoulder stabilizers
